units.meaning: Administrative publication and revision metadata with no substantive operational rule.
Explains that U.S. passports, Form FS-240, and Form DS-2060 are printed in all uppercase letters following ICAO recommendations.

source_spans.quote: In accordance with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) recommendations, U.S. passports, form FS-240, and form DS-2060 are printed in all uppercase letters.

units.meaning: Explains the technical consequence that multipart names printed in uppercase appear as a single word unless separated by spaces.

source_spans.quote: Printing a name with multiple parts in uppercase letters causes the name to appear as one word unless the parts are separated with spaces.

units.meaning: If an applicant has a multipart name, personnel are obligated to determine how the name will appear on the document.

source_spans.quote: Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:

units.meaning: When determining the appearance of a multipart name, if the applicant's previous passport contained a space, personnel are advised to add a space on the current application.

source_spans.quote: If the applicant's previous passport had a space, you should add a space on the current application;
Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:

units.meaning: When determining the appearance of a multipart name, if the applicant lacks a prior passport but their citizenship/nationality evidence or ID has a space, personnel are advised to add a space on the current application.

source_spans.quote: If the applicant does not have a previous passport and the applicant's evidence of U.S. citizenship/non-citizen U.S. nationality or ID has a space, you should add a space on the current application; or
Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:

units.meaning: When determining the appearance of a multipart name, personnel are authorized to add or remove space in accordance with the applicant's stated preference if the applicant communicates a clear preference verbally or in writing.

source_spans.quote: If the applicant expresses a clear preference to add or remove space, either verbally or in writing, you may add or remove it per the applicant's preference.
Consequently, if the applicant has a name with multiple parts, you must determine how the name will appear:

units.meaning: When receiving applications from multiple family members, personnel should space their last names consistently, except when an individual family member explicitly expresses a preference for different spacing.

source_spans.quote: NOTE: If you receive applications from several family members, you should space the last names consistently, unless a family member expresses a clear preference for a different spacing.

units.meaning: In the case of special-issuance passports, the spacing of an eligible family member's last name should correspond to the spacing of the sponsor's last name.

source_spans.quote: NOTE: For special-issuance passports, the spacing of an eligible family member's last name should match the spacing of the last name of the sponsor.

units.meaning: Issues regarding name spacing generally do not justify rewriting a passport, except when the Department failed to follow the applicant's clearly expressed preference.

source_spans.quote: Name spacing issues are generally not sufficient cause to rewrite a passport, unless the Department disregarded the applicant's clear preference (see 8 FAM 1001.2).

units.meaning: Personnel are required to convert Arabic ordinal numbers in names to Roman numerals (e.g., changing '2nd' to 'II' and '3rd' to 'III').
